clinicalPearls: Gestational trophoblastic disease is a spectrum of proliferative disorders of placental trophoblast ranging from benign hydatidiform mole to malignant gestational trophoblastic neoplasia including choriocarcinoma
A complete mole usually arises from fertilisation of an ovum lacking maternal genetic material and contains no fetal tissue, whereas a partial mole is typically triploid with some fetal parts

Classic presentation includes irregular vaginal bleeding in early pregnancy, a uterus large for dates, markedly elevated hCG, and sometimes early or severe hyperemesis or pre-eclampsia before twenty weeks
Ultrasound may show a vesicular or snowstorm appearance with absent or abnormal fetal development, and diagnosis is confirmed histologically
Uterine evacuation by suction curettage is the treatment for molar pregnancy, followed by structured monitoring of serial hCG to detect persistent disease
Persistently elevated or rising hCG after evacuation indicates gestational trophoblastic neoplasia, which is highly chemosensitive and generally curable even when metastatic
Reliable contraception during hCG surveillance is essential because a new pregnancy would obscure the marker used to detect persistent disease
Choriocarcinoma can follow any pregnancy, including normal or ectopic, and may present with metastatic symptoms such as haemoptysis or neurological signs
reference.pathophysiology: Gestational trophoblastic disease results from abnormal fertilisation and proliferation of trophoblastic tissue. A complete mole typically arises when an anucleate ovum is fertilised and the paternal chromosomes duplicate, giving a diploid androgenetic genome with swollen avascular chorionic villi and no fetus, while a partial mole usually results from dispermic fertilisation producing a triploid conceptus with focal villous change and a nonviable fetus. Excessive trophoblast produces very high hCG. In gestational trophoblastic neoplasia, trophoblast invades the myometrium and vasculature, and choriocarcinoma disseminates haematogenously, favouring the lungs, brain, and liver.
additionalDifferentials: Normal early intrauterine pregnancy with bleeding
additionalInvestigations: Quantitative serum hCG, which is often markedly elevated
Pelvic ultrasound to assess for molar features and fetal tissue
Histological examination of evacuated tissue, with ploidy and immunostaining where needed
Serial hCG monitoring after evacuation to detect persistent disease
Chest imaging and cross-sectional staging when neoplasia or metastasis is suspected
Baseline full blood count, renal, liver and thyroid function given possible hCG-driven thyroid effects
redFlags: Rising or plateauing hCG after evacuation signalling gestational trophoblastic neoplasia requiring urgent oncology referral
Heavy vaginal bleeding with haemodynamic compromise
Respiratory symptoms or haemoptysis suggesting pulmonary metastases
Neurological signs suggesting cerebral metastatic choriocarcinoma
Pre-eclampsia, thyrotoxic features, or hyperemesis occurring unusually early in pregnancy
reference.prognosis: Most hydatidiform moles are cured by evacuation alone, and even when gestational trophoblastic neoplasia develops it is one of the most curable malignancies, with excellent survival when managed in specialist centres using chemotherapy guided by prognostic scoring. Outcome depends on prompt diagnosis, adherence to hCG surveillance, and risk stratification, with high-risk and heavily metastatic disease requiring more intensive multi-agent treatment.
pitfalls: Failing to arrange structured hCG follow-up after evacuation
Allowing pregnancy during surveillance, which masks persistent disease
Missing early or atypical pre-eclampsia and hyperthyroid features as clues to molar pregnancy
Not considering choriocarcinoma in a woman with metastatic disease and any recent pregnancy
Assuming a benign miscarriage without histological examination of tissue
management: Evacuate a molar pregnancy by suction curettage as first-line treatment
Give anti-D prophylaxis to rhesus-negative women and avoid oxytocic augmentation before evacuation
Undertake structured serial hCG monitoring after evacuation to detect persistent disease
Advise reliable contraception and avoidance of pregnancy until hCG has normalised during follow-up
Escalate to chemotherapy when hCG plateaus or rises, indicating gestational trophoblastic neoplasia
Register and manage the patient at a specialist trophoblastic disease centre
Manage associated hCG-driven hyperthyroidism, early pre-eclampsia, and anaemia
